hook: From a quiet Sunday morning over the green water of Pearl Harbor in December nineteen forty-one, to the still grey deck of a battleship in Tokyo Bay in September nineteen forty-five, the long Pacific war, told softly, so you can rest.
narration:
Imagine you are standing on the small wooden lanai of a house in the hills above the harbor. The morning is warm, but not yet hot. The trade wind has come up off the sea and is moving the leaves of a hibiscus by the steps. Below you, in the long, sheltered water, the grey ships of the United States Pacific Fleet lie at their moorings, their awnings rigged for Sunday, their flags not yet hoisted. A bugle, somewhere on one of the battleships, sounds the call for morning colors. A church bell rings in the small Hawaiian town behind you. The date is the seventh of December, nineteen forty-one. In a few minutes, the long Pacific war will begin. You have not yet heard the engines.

Tonight, we will follow that war from this still morning in Hawaii, all the way to a battleship deck in Tokyo Bay, four years away. There is no urgency in this journey. The years will pass at their own pace. The names of the islands and the names of the ships and the names of the men will pass through the story as they came, and they will not be tested. You are welcome to drift, to come and go, to fall asleep at any time. The story will keep itself.

Before the engines come, a word about how the war began. For ten years, since the seizure of Manchuria in nineteen thirty-one, the Empire of Japan has been at war on the Asian mainland. By nineteen forty, Japanese armies hold the eastern seaboard of China and most of Indochina. Their navy is the third largest in the world, their pilots among the best trained, their carriers the most modern. Through the autumn of nineteen forty-one, the Japanese government, under the army-led cabinet of Prime Minister Tojo, has decided that an embargo of oil, iron, and steel by the United States, Britain, and the Netherlands cannot be borne, and that war must come before the stocks run dry. The plan, prepared by an admiral named Yamamoto, who had once studied at Harvard and watched Detroit make automobiles, is to strike the American fleet in its base, while at the same moment moving south against the British in Malaya, the Dutch in the Indies, the Americans in the Philippines, the British and Australians in Hong Kong and the Bismarcks. Yamamoto is not certain Japan can win a long war. He hopes only to win the first six months and to negotiate from the strength of those gains. He has told his prime minister so, plainly. The plan goes forward anyway.

The ships you see in the harbor below you are seven battleships, the Nevada, the Arizona, the West Virginia, the Tennessee, the Maryland, the Oklahoma, the California, with the Pennsylvania in dry dock — eight in all. The carriers are away. Lexington has gone west to Midway with planes for the marines there. Enterprise, returning from Wake, is a few hundred miles to the east, due in tomorrow. Saratoga is on the West Coast for refit. The men aboard the battleships are cooking breakfast, polishing brightwork, writing letters home, dressing for inspection. Some are still in their bunks. Above the harbor, the morning patrol planes are routine. A radar set at Opana, on the north shore of Oahu, has just picked up a large echo coming in from the north. The two privates at the screen report it. The duty officer at the central plot tells them it is probably a flight of B-17s expected from California. He says, gently, not to worry about it. They sign off and lock up the trailer.

At seven fifty-five in the morning, the first Japanese aircraft come in low over Battleship Row. There are one hundred and eighty-three of them in the first wave, dive bombers, level bombers, torpedo planes, fighters, launched from six aircraft carriers two hundred and twenty miles to the north. They have been listening to a Honolulu radio station to fix their bearings. The first torpedo strikes the Oklahoma at eight zero-one. Within the next twenty minutes, the West Virginia takes seven torpedo hits and settles to the harbor mud. The Oklahoma rolls completely over. The Arizona is hit by a heavy armor-piercing bomb that penetrates her forward magazine, and at six minutes past eight she explodes, a great rising cloud of black smoke and white fragments, and one thousand one hundred and seventy-seven men aboard her are killed in a single instant. The Nevada, alone of the battleships, manages to get steam up and underway, and her crew tries to take her out of the harbor. Japanese pilots, seeing her move, swing onto her, and she is hit so heavily that her captain runs her aground rather than let her sink in the channel. By ten o'clock, the second wave has come and gone. Two thousand four hundred and three Americans are dead. Half the Pacific Fleet's battleships are sunk or settled. The harbor is on fire from end to end.

We put a great deal of care into bringing you these long stories. If you have settled in and you are enjoying this, a quiet like helps the channel reach more people who like to fall asleep to history, and subscribing tells us to keep producing them. Thank you for staying with us.

Far to the south and west, on that same day across the international date line, it is already the eighth of December. The Japanese plan unfolds at every point at once. Bombers from Formosa attack the American air force on the Philippines while its planes are still parked at Clark Field, where General MacArthur has hesitated all morning, and most of his bombers and fighters are destroyed in their first hour. Other Japanese landings come ashore at Luzon, at Mindanao, at Davao. Singapore is bombed. Hong Kong is attacked from the mainland by Japanese troops who have crossed the border from Canton. In Malaya, two divisions of the Twenty-Fifth Army, under a small, careful general named Yamashita, land at Kota Bharu and at the Thai ports, and begin a campaign that will, in seventy days, carry them six hundred miles down a peninsula the British defenders had said was impassable.

The Royal Navy, that same week, sends two of its great ships north from Singapore. The battleship Prince of Wales, which only half a year before had carried Winston Churchill to meet Roosevelt in Newfoundland, and the old battlecruiser Repulse, sail without air cover into the Gulf of Siam to find the Japanese landing fleet. They are spotted, instead, by Japanese torpedo bombers from Saigon. On the morning of the tenth of December, both ships are sunk in less than two hours. Eight hundred and forty British sailors are lost. Admiral Tom Phillips goes down with his flagship. The era of the battleship as the ruler of the seas, which had lasted in some form for three hundred years, ends in the South China Sea on a clear, hot December morning. From this date forward, the warship that matters in the Pacific will be the aircraft carrier.

Through the rest of December and through January, the bad news comes in by daily cable. Wake Island, defended by a few hundred marines and a handful of fighter planes, holds out from the eighth of December until the twenty-third, sinking two Japanese destroyers and damaging others, before being overrun. The marines on Wake send a final radio message that has been remembered ever since: send us more Japs. Hong Kong falls on Christmas Day after seventeen days of fighting. Manila is declared an open city by MacArthur and the American and Philippine armies withdraw to the Bataan Peninsula and the small fortified island of Corregidor in Manila Bay. The Japanese take Manila on the second of January. They begin the long siege of Bataan and Corregidor, which will go on, in conditions of growing hunger and disease, until April and May.

Further west, in the high green country of upper Burma, Japanese armies break a thin British and Indian line on the Salween River and push north toward the great supply road called the Burma Road, the only land route by which American aid can still reach the Chinese Nationalist armies of Chiang Kai-shek. By the spring of nineteen forty-two, Burma will be held by the Japanese, and the Burma Road will be cut. Chinese supplies will have to come, after that, by air, over the high passes of the Himalayas, what the pilots will call the Hump.

In Singapore, the great British fortress, said before the war to be impregnable, the campaign comes to its bitter conclusion in February. Yamashita's divisions cross the narrow Johore Strait at night on rubber boats and small landing craft. The British defenders, exhausted from three months of retreat, run out of water in the city's reservoirs as Japanese artillery walks across the holding tanks. On the fifteenth of February nineteen forty-two, the British general Percival surrenders Singapore to Yamashita in a small upstairs room at the Ford factory at Bukit Timah. Eighty thousand British, Indian, and Australian soldiers go into Japanese captivity. It is the largest surrender in British military history. Many of them will be marched north to work on the railway between Burma and Thailand, the line that will become known to the world as the death railway, where, over the next three years, more than a hundred thousand prisoners and forced laborers will die.

In the Dutch East Indies, the great oilfield prize, the Allies make a last naval stand in the Java Sea on the twenty-seventh of February. A scratch fleet of Dutch, British, American, and Australian cruisers and destroyers under the Dutch admiral Doorman meets a heavier Japanese force escorting troop transports. After a long, confused, slow afternoon and night battle, the Allied fleet is annihilated. Doorman goes down with his flagship, signaling I am attacking, follow me. Java is invaded a week later. The Dutch government in exile in Batavia signs a surrender on the eighth of March. The four-century Dutch presence in the Indies ends in a hot week of fighting and a long four-year captivity for the Dutch families who do not get out in time.

On Bataan, on the ninth of April nineteen forty-two, the seventy-six thousand surviving American and Filipino troops, ill with malaria and dysentery, on quarter rations and lower, surrender to the Japanese. They are marched, in the heat, sixty-five miles north to a railhead at San Fernando. On the way, men who fall behind are shot or bayoneted. Men who beg for water at village wells are killed. Some Japanese guards behave decently. Many do not. Of the seventy-six thousand who set out, perhaps twenty thousand never finish. The march will be remembered, in the words used afterward, as a war crime. On Corregidor, the small island fortress in the bay, the American garrison holds out a month longer, until the sixth of May, when the last reserves of food and water are gone and General Wainwright, who has succeeded MacArthur, surrenders the island. MacArthur himself, on direct orders from the President, has been ordered out by motor torpedo boat through the Japanese blockade in March. He has reached Australia and made his famous, simple promise: I shall return.

This is the dark first half year that Yamamoto had warned of and that he had hoped to use to bargain. The Japanese empire, by the spring of nineteen forty-two, runs from the Aleutians, in the cold north, down through Wake and the Marshalls, across the Carolines and the Marianas, to New Guinea and the Solomons in the south, and west through the Indies, Malaya, Burma, all the way to the borders of India. It is the greatest expanse of territory ever held by a single Asian state. The cost has been remarkably small. The defending forces have been overrun almost everywhere. The Japanese carriers, the six great fleet carriers under Admiral Nagumo that had launched the strike at Pearl Harbor, have ranged from Hawaii to the Indian Ocean, sinking a British carrier and battering the British Eastern Fleet to ineffectiveness. By April nineteen forty-two, the Japanese navy has not lost a single capital ship.

But the American carriers, the three that had been away from Pearl Harbor on the day of the attack, are still at sea. Through January and February, they make small raids on the outer Japanese islands, the Marshalls and the Gilberts and Wake, almost more for morale than for damage. In April, sixteen American B-25 medium bombers, under a former racing pilot named Doolittle, take off from the deck of the carrier Hornet, six hundred miles east of Japan, and fly low over the Japanese home islands, dropping their small bomb loads on Tokyo, Yokohama, Nagoya, and Kobe. The damage is light. The crews fly on, most of them, to land in China, where Chinese peasants help them escape and pay for that help in reprisal massacres by Japanese armies. The Doolittle Raid does almost no military damage. It does, however, change the calculations of the Japanese high command. The home islands have been touched. To prevent another such raid, the navy is given approval for a campaign that Yamamoto has been pressing — to draw the American carriers into a decisive battle near a small atoll halfway across the ocean, called Midway.

Before Midway comes a smaller, stranger battle in the Coral Sea, north of Australia, in early May. Japanese forces have set out to seize Port Moresby, the last Allied base on New Guinea, and a small place called Tulagi in the Solomons. American codebreakers have read enough of the Japanese naval code to know they are coming. The carriers Lexington and Yorktown sail to meet them. For four days, from the fourth to the eighth of May, the two carrier groups feel for each other across hundreds of miles of empty sea. They never see one another's ships. Their planes meet in the air, and over the open water, and on each other's flight decks. The Lexington is crippled by torpedoes and bombs and finally sunk by her own destroyers in the evening of the eighth. The Yorktown is badly damaged. The Japanese light carrier Shoho is sunk in the morning of the seventh. The bigger carriers Shokaku and Zuikaku are damaged or have lost their air groups. The Port Moresby invasion is turned back. It is the first naval battle in history in which the opposing ships never sight one another. It is the first strategic check the Japanese have suffered. And it has, although neither side fully knows yet, removed Shokaku and Zuikaku from the list of Japanese carriers available for the great blow at Midway, four weeks away.

The Battle of Midway, on the third, fourth, and fifth of June nineteen forty-two, is one of those battles around which whole later wars seem to pivot. Yamamoto has assembled a great fleet, nearly two hundred ships, and divided it into three task forces: a covering force of battleships, a secondary force aimed at the Aleutian Islands far to the north, and a striking force of four fleet carriers, under Nagumo, ordered to bomb Midway atoll into ruin and to draw out and destroy whatever American carriers respond. The Americans, under Admiral Nimitz at Pearl Harbor, have read enough of the Japanese plan from intercepted radio traffic to set their own ambush. The carriers Enterprise and Hornet, under Admiral Spruance, and the patched-together Yorktown, under Admiral Fletcher, are waiting north of Midway when Nagumo arrives.

Through the morning of the fourth of June, Nagumo's planes attack Midway, and Midway's planes, mostly old and ill-handled, attack Nagumo's carriers and are mostly shot down. American carrier torpedo bombers, forty-one of them, attack Nagumo's force in successive small flights, and again, almost all of them are destroyed. By ten o'clock in the morning, Nagumo has been told four times that the American carriers do not seem to be present, and he has begun to rearm his planes for a second strike on Midway atoll, with the bombs and torpedoes piled on his hangar decks. At ten twenty, while his deck crews are in the middle of this rearming, three squadrons of American dive bombers from the Enterprise and the Yorktown — fifty-four planes — appear above the Japanese fleet, almost unopposed because the Japanese fighter cover is down low after the torpedo attacks. In six minutes, three of Nagumo's four fleet carriers, the Akagi, the Kaga, and the Soryu, are mortally hit. The fourth, the Hiryu, manages a counter-strike that hits the Yorktown twice, but in the late afternoon she too is found and bombed by Enterprise's planes, and burns through the night. By the morning of the fifth of June, four of Japan's six great fleet carriers and three hundred and thirty-two of her best naval pilots are gone. The strategic balance of the Pacific war, in those six minutes, has shifted. Yamamoto's hoped-for short war is over. The long one begins.

In the weeks after Midway, the Allies turn from defense to a slow, careful counterattack, beginning at the southern edge of the Japanese arc, in the Solomon Islands. On the seventh of August nineteen forty-two, the United States First Marine Division, under General Vandegrift, lands on the long jungle island of Guadalcanal and on the smaller islands across the channel, Tulagi, Gavutu, and Tanambogo. The marines come ashore, in many places, almost unopposed. A few hundred Japanese construction troops on Guadalcanal, building an airfield, melt into the bush. The marines move inland and seize the unfinished strip, which they will name Henderson Field, after a marine pilot killed at Midway. Within days, however, things begin to come apart.

A Japanese cruiser force, under Admiral Mikawa, slips down from Rabaul on the night of the eighth of August and ambushes the Allied warships covering the landing in a confused, brief night battle off the small island of Savo. In thirty minutes, four heavy cruisers — three American and one Australian — are sunk. The Vincennes, the Quincy, the Astoria, the Canberra. More than a thousand sailors die. The American transports, still unloading on the beach, are now without naval protection, and the next morning the rest of them sail away, leaving the marines on the island with only part of their supplies. For the next four months, Guadalcanal will be one of the loneliest places in the war. The marines will hold the airfield. The Japanese will land troops at night by destroyer convoys the marines call the Tokyo Express. The two sides will fight, in the bush, in the jungle, in the rain, around a small ridge that the marines call Edson's Ridge after the colonel who held it, around the Matanikau River, around a cape called Cape Esperance.

At sea, off the island, six major naval battles will be fought in those four months: Savo, the Eastern Solomons, Cape Esperance, Santa Cruz, the two nights of the naval Battle of Guadalcanal in November, and Tassafaronga. American battleships under Admiral Lee fight a Japanese battleship in the dark of the fourteenth of November and sink her, in the only direct battleship-to-battleship action of the Pacific war. The American carriers Wasp and Hornet are sunk. The carrier Enterprise is damaged twice. The Japanese battleships Hiei and Kirishima are sunk. By the end of November, the Japanese cannot keep their men supplied. By the new year, they are starving. By the seventh of February nineteen forty-three, the last Japanese troops have been evacuated from the island by destroyer at night, and Guadalcanal is in American hands. The cost on both sides has been about thirty thousand dead. The lesson, learned slowly by the marines and sailors and pilots who lived through it, is that the Japanese soldier and sailor are not invincible, and that they can be beaten in fair fights, given enough men and ships and time. The lesson learned in Tokyo is harsher. The carriers cannot be replaced. The pilots cannot be replaced. America can replace both, in numbers that grow each month.

Through nineteen forty-three, the long, slow Allied counterattack moves forward on two roads. In the southwest Pacific, MacArthur's forces, operating from Australia, push west and north along the spine of New Guinea, in a series of small amphibious leaps from one undefended bay to the next, called by his officers the leapfrog strategy. Buna and Gona on the north coast of New Guinea fall in early nineteen forty-three after a hard, malarial fight by Australian and American troops. Lae and Salamaua follow in September. Finschhafen falls in October. The point of these operations is not to destroy the Japanese garrisons but to step around them, leaving them isolated to wither while the war moves on. In the central Pacific, Admiral Nimitz at Pearl Harbor begins the long climb up the island chain that will become the main road to Tokyo. In November of nineteen forty-three, the Second Marine Division lands on the small heavily fortified atoll of Tarawa, in the Gilberts. In seventy-six hours of fighting, more than a thousand marines are killed and two thousand wounded on a piece of land smaller than New York's Central Park. The defending Japanese garrison, four thousand five hundred strong, fights almost to the last man. Tarawa is the model that worries the public, and that the marines themselves study afterward, looking for ways to make such an attack less costly the next time. They will need to make many such attacks.

In the air over the home islands and over the slowly-shrinking Japanese empire, a different campaign is gathering. From bases in eastern China, B-29 Superfortresses, the largest bombers of the war, begin small raids on western Japan in nineteen forty-four. From the Marianas, after their capture, the same B-29s begin a much heavier campaign against Japanese cities. The early raids, at high altitude, with high-explosive bombs, are not very effective; the jet stream over Japan is unexpectedly strong, and bomb patterns scatter for miles. In March of nineteen forty-five, a new commander of the Twenty-First Air Force, General Curtis LeMay, will change the doctrine — strip the bombers of their guns, fly low at night, and use mostly incendiary bombs against the wooden cities. The first such raid, on the night of the ninth and tenth of March, will burn out sixteen square miles of Tokyo and kill more than a hundred thousand people in a single night. The fire raids will continue, city by city, through the spring and into the summer.

In February of nineteen forty-four, Nimitz's forces take Kwajalein and Eniwetok in the Marshalls, almost in passing. In June, they make their largest amphibious leap so far, to the Mariana Islands. The marines and the army land on Saipan on the fifteenth of June. The Japanese fleet, under Admiral Ozawa, comes out to fight, in the largest carrier battle since Midway. On the nineteenth of June nineteen forty-four, in the open sea east of the Marianas, American fighters under Admiral Mitscher meet the Japanese strikes in the air, and shoot down so many of them that the American pilots call it the Marianas Turkey Shoot. By the end of the next day, two more Japanese carriers have been sunk by submarines, and a third by an air strike at extreme range. The carrier arm of the Imperial Japanese Navy, after this battle, will never again be a serious factor in the Pacific war. Saipan itself is taken on the ninth of July, after weeks of fighting that include, at the end, the suicide of Japanese civilians who throw themselves and their children from the cliffs at the northern tip rather than fall into American hands. Tinian and Guam follow within the next month. The B-29 bases that will burn the cities of Japan are now in American territory.

In October of nineteen forty-four, MacArthur, fulfilling his old promise, returns to the Philippines. The American Sixth Army lands at Leyte on the twentieth of October. MacArthur himself wades ashore from a landing craft a few hours later, broadcasts a short, formal speech beginning with the words people of the Philippines, I have returned, and walks up the beach in his tropical khakis. The reaction in Tokyo is to commit the entire remaining Japanese fleet to a single complicated plan, called Sho-Go, to converge on Leyte Gulf from three directions and destroy the American invasion force. The plan results in the largest naval engagement of the war, and perhaps in history, fought across the Philippine archipelago over four days, the twenty-third to the twenty-sixth of October nineteen forty-four. There are four separate actions: the submarine ambush of a Japanese center force in the Palawan Passage, the air-sea battle in the Sibuyan Sea, the night battle in the narrow Surigao Strait, and the strange, panic-edged action off the small American escort carriers near the island of Samar. By the end of those four days, the Japanese navy has lost three battleships, including the great Musashi, sunk by air attack in the Sibuyan; four carriers; ten cruisers; and a dozen destroyers. The American navy has lost an escort carrier, two destroyer escorts, and a fleet destroyer. From this point on, the Imperial Japanese Navy, as a fighting force, has effectively ceased to exist.

In the same battle, the Japanese first use, with formal sanction from the high command, the kamikaze, the divine wind, the deliberately suicidal aircraft attack. The first organized kamikaze unit, under Vice Admiral Onishi, attacks the American escort carriers off Samar on the morning of the twenty-fifth of October. The carrier Saint Lo is hit and sunks. From this date forward, until the end of the war, the kamikaze will be the single most lethal Japanese weapon at sea, killing thousands of Allied sailors and damaging hundreds of ships, but it will not change the strategic outcome. It is a weapon born of a kind of despair as much as of strategy.

The ground campaign in the Philippines, after Leyte, goes on through the rest of nineteen forty-four and into the summer of nineteen forty-five. Luzon is invaded on the ninth of January nineteen forty-five, at the same Lingayen Gulf where the Japanese had come ashore three years before. The Sixth Army drives south through the central plain. Manila is reached at the start of February. The fight for the city is one of the worst of the war, a slow building-by-building battle in which Japanese marines, ordered to die in place, hold the old walled district of Intramuros and the great government buildings to the last. By the end of the month, much of Manila has been destroyed by artillery and demolition. More than a hundred thousand Filipino civilians have been killed in the fighting, in the largest urban battle of the Pacific war.

While Manila burns, far to the north, Marines of the Fifth Amphibious Corps land on the small volcanic island of Iwo Jima, halfway between the Marianas and Tokyo. The island is barely eight square miles, but it has three airfields and a single tall extinct volcano, Mount Suribachi, at its southern tip. The Japanese garrison, twenty-one thousand men under General Kuribayashi, has prepared for this moment with eleven miles of underground tunnels, with strong points cut into the volcanic rock, with carefully ranged artillery on every part of the small open beach. The marines come ashore on the nineteenth of February nineteen forty-five. The black volcanic sand is so soft that men sink to their knees as they walk. By the end of the first day, more than two thousand marines are dead or wounded. The fight will go on for thirty-six days. On the morning of the twenty-third of February, after four days of climbing, six marines reach the summit of Suribachi and raise a small American flag. A few hours later, they raise a second, larger flag, and a photographer from the Associated Press named Joe Rosenthal takes a single quick exposure. The image will become, perhaps, the most reproduced photograph of the twentieth century. Of the six marines in it, three will be killed before the battle ends. Of the seventy thousand marines who land on the island, twenty-six thousand will be killed or wounded. Of the twenty-one thousand Japanese, all but a few hundred will die. Iwo Jima becomes the only battle of the Pacific war in which the American casualties are higher than the Japanese.

In the spring of nineteen forty-five, the last great amphibious landing of the war comes at the long, mountainous island of Okinawa, three hundred miles south of the Japanese home islands. The Tenth Army, under General Buckner, with marines and army divisions together, lands on the first of April. The landing itself is almost unopposed. The Japanese garrison, under General Ushijima, has chosen to fight not on the beaches but in the rugged ridge country of the southern part of the island, where a series of fortified lines, the Shuri Line at their center, makes a slow, systematic defense possible. The campaign that follows will last eighty-two days, until the twenty-second of June. It is the largest battle of the Pacific theater. It costs the lives of more than twelve thousand Americans and more than a hundred thousand Japanese soldiers, and perhaps as many as a hundred and fifty thousand Okinawan civilians, who are caught in the fighting, used by both sides, drafted into local defense by the Japanese, killed by artillery and by mass suicide encouraged by Japanese officers in the cliffs of the southern coast. At sea, off the island, the kamikaze attacks reach their peak. Almost five thousand American sailors are killed by kamikaze and bomb hits during the campaign, more than the marines lose ashore. The kamikaze attacks include the sortie of the great Japanese battleship Yamato, which sails on a one-way trip from the home islands toward Okinawa with fuel for only one direction; she is found by American carrier aircraft on the seventh of April and sunk in two hours. Three thousand of her four thousand crewmen are killed. General Buckner himself is killed on the eighteenth of June, by a Japanese artillery shell, the highest-ranking American officer killed in the war. General Ushijima commits suicide in his command cave on the twenty-second of June. Okinawa is the warning. Japan is fighting harder, not weaker, as the Allies come closer to her home soil.

Through the spring and early summer of nineteen forty-five, the planners in Washington and on Guam are looking at what comes next. The plan, called Operation Downfall, is the invasion of the Japanese home islands themselves, beginning with Kyushu in November nineteen forty-five and continuing with Honshu and the Tokyo plain in the spring of nineteen forty-six. The estimates of casualties for an invasion of the home islands run, depending on which staff produces them, from a quarter of a million Allied dead and wounded to as many as a million; Japanese military and civilian losses are expected to be several times that. Through July, the Imperial Japanese Army gathers some two and a half million men in the home islands and trains civilian militias, including women and children, to resist with bamboo spears if necessary. Cabinet meetings in Tokyo, throughout that summer, debate but do not agree on whether to seek terms.

Far away, in the desert of New Mexico, on the morning of the sixteenth of July, in a place called Alamogordo, a small group of physicists and engineers detonate the first atomic bomb in human history. It is the result of three years of work by the Manhattan Project, of the labor of a hundred and thirty thousand people, and a budget of two billion dollars, almost all of it kept secret from the American public and from the rank and file of the army itself. The desert sky lights up white and then orange and then red. A column of fire rises miles into the air. The scientist in charge, J. Robert Oppenheimer, will say afterward that he thought of a line from the Bhagavad Gita, that he had become death, the destroyer of worlds. President Truman, who has only been president since the death of Roosevelt in April, is at the Potsdam Conference in occupied Germany when he is told. The decision he must make is whether to use this new weapon against Japan to try to end the war without an invasion. He decides to use it.

On the morning of the sixth of August nineteen forty-five, a single B-29, named Enola Gay, flying from Tinian in the Marianas, drops a uranium bomb on the city of Hiroshima. The bomb detonates, by design, at about two thousand feet over the city center. The flash, the heat, the blast, and the firestorm that follows kill some seventy thousand people in the first day, and as many more in the weeks and months and years that follow, of burns, of radiation, of cancer. Three days later, on the ninth of August, a plutonium bomb is dropped on the city of Nagasaki, killing perhaps forty thousand more in the first day. Between the two attacks, on the eighth of August, the Soviet Union declares war on Japan and invades Manchuria, where a great Japanese army has been kept in place against this contingency. The Soviet armies advance hundreds of miles in a few days. The combination of the new American weapon, the Soviet entry, and the steady pressure of the conventional bombing of the cities at last forces a decision in Tokyo. The Emperor Hirohito, on the night of the ninth and tenth of August, breaks with the long Japanese tradition that the throne does not intervene in cabinet decisions, and tells his ministers that they must accept the Allied terms. After several more days of debate, an attempted coup by army officers who refuse to accept surrender, and a second imperial intervention, the decision holds. On the fifteenth of August, at noon Tokyo time, in a recorded radio address, the Emperor speaks to his subjects for the first time in their lives, in a formal classical Japanese that many of them do not entirely understand, telling them that the war situation has developed not necessarily to Japan's advantage and that the unbearable must be borne. The war is over.

On the morning of the second of September nineteen forty-five, in Tokyo Bay, in mist and a thin grey sun, the formal surrender is signed on the deck of the American battleship Missouri. The flag of Commodore Perry, who had sailed into the same bay in eighteen fifty-three to open Japan to the West, is on display, brought from Annapolis for the occasion. Japanese officials, in top hats and morning coats, stand on one side of a small wooden table. American, British, Soviet, Chinese, French, Dutch, Australian, New Zealand, and Canadian officers stand on the other. The Japanese foreign minister, Mamoru Shigemitsu, leaning on a cane because of the leg he had lost to a bomb in Shanghai years before, signs first. General MacArthur, as Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signs second, with five different pens, which he distributes to officers around him. Above the harbor, twelve hundred carrier aircraft and Superfortresses pass in a great long formation. The instrument of surrender is closed. MacArthur steps to a microphone and says, simply, that these proceedings are now closed.

In the years that follow, the men who have lived through the long Pacific war will go home. Some return on troopships to San Francisco, to San Diego, to Brisbane, to Sydney, to Wellington. Some march back along the muddy roads of New Guinea and Burma. The prisoners come last, the men who have spent three and four years in Japanese camps, in the railway country of Thailand, in the coal mines of northern Japan, in Manila and Singapore and Java. Many are skeletal. Some are blind from beriberi or unable to walk. They are flown out, in many places, on transport planes that carry them straight to base hospitals in Manila and Australia and Hawaii. The American soldiers who have walked through the ruins of the Japanese cities for the first weeks of the occupation describe what they have seen in language that does not always come back into common speech. The Japanese soldiers who survive the long retreat from Manchuria, from Korea, from the Pacific outposts, return to a country with two of its great cities reduced to ash, with ration lines on every street, with the homes of their childhoods sometimes simply gone.

The great islands and the small ones return slowly to themselves. In the lagoons of the central Pacific, the carriers and the destroyers and the battleships of nineteen forty-five sit out the long peace, some of them mothballed at Bremerton or Yokosuka, some of them sunk in deep water as targets for atomic tests at Bikini in nineteen forty-six. The names of those ships — Enterprise, Hornet, Lexington, Saratoga, Yorktown, Wasp, Essex — pass slowly out of the active rolls. The men who flew from their decks grow old in towns from Maine to California, from Sydney to Wellington, telling, when they can, the stories of long, hot afternoons over empty water, when the radio called the bearings and the bombs went down through the clouds onto a deck a hundred miles below them.

The atolls themselves are still there. Pearl Harbor, on its quiet Sunday mornings now, is a place of memorials, of small white boats taking visitors out to a long white concrete bridge over the rusted bones of the Arizona. Midway is a wildlife refuge, where the seabirds of the central Pacific raise their chicks on the same coral beaches that were bombed in June nineteen forty-two. Iwo Jima is a Japanese island again, with a single careful monument to the marines and a single careful monument to the Japanese garrison. Okinawa is a place of long beaches and small towns, of American military bases that remain to this day, of cane fields and pineapple groves growing again over the old ridges. Tokyo is a city of glass and steel that none of the men who flew over it in nineteen forty-five would now recognize. Nagasaki and Hiroshima are cities once more, with their own quiet parks at the centers of where the bombs fell, with single bent steel domes left standing as reminders, with thousands of paper cranes folded and brought every year by school children who read the stories.

This is the long Pacific war, told as gently as it can be told. The morning at Pearl Harbor. The fall of the Philippines and Singapore and Java. The battle in the Coral Sea and the six minutes off Midway. The long fight at Guadalcanal and the slow climb up the island chain. The Marianas and the Philippine Sea. The return to the Philippines and the four-day fight in Leyte Gulf. The black sand of Iwo Jima and the long ridges of Okinawa. The desert flash at Alamogordo and the two cities. The deck of the Missouri in the September mist.

The sea, after all of this, is quiet again. The trade wind still moves the leaves of the hibiscus by the steps of small houses on small islands. The carriers that survive grow old. The men who came home grow old, and many of them do not speak of the war, and some of them do, in books and in oral histories that we still read. The men who did not come home lie under white crosses in Honolulu, in Manila, in Hawaii's National Memorial Cemetery in the Punchbowl, in a long quiet ridge above the city. The Japanese dead lie in the small wooden shrines of their towns, with names brushed on long thin paper tablets, in places like Hiroshima and Tokyo and Yokohama and the small fishing villages of the Inland Sea. The Pacific, the great ocean, runs east to west and west to east, in slow long blue swells, as it always has. Somewhere on it, tonight, a freighter is moving toward Yokohama, with a lamp burning at its bow, and the lamp keeps the same gentle steady light that the lanterns of the small island fishermen kept three hundred and four hundred years ago, before any of this happened.

We put a great deal of care into bringing you this. If it has helped you rest, a quiet like helps the channel, and subscribing tells us to keep making more long, soft histories like this one. Thank you for staying with us tonight. Sleep well.
